newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan keeping Deng Xiaoping health vigil.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan keeping Deng Xiaoping health vigil.

text.p: Taiwan's government and military on Tuesday said they were on alert for further reports on Chinese paramount leader Deng Xiaoping's deteriorating health and were closely watching the situation.
State television said the Taiwan military was on alert, but it has not detected any unusual movements of mainland troops.
"The military is closely following situation on the mainland, and carefully monitoring communist armed forces' activities," military spokesman Kung Fan-ting told reporters at a press briefing.

Chang King-yuh, chairman of the cabinet's Mainland Affairs Council, which formulates Taiwan's policies towards China, was quoted by the mass circulation United Daily News as describing Deng's health as "serious".

"According to sources from relevant authorities, (Deng's) condition this time is indeed very serious," the United Daily News quoted Chang as saying. He gave no details, but said Taiwan had full knowledge of the situation.
Taiwan and China have been diplomatic rivals since the Chinese civil war split them in 1949.
Sources in Beijing on Monday said Deng's deteriorating health had led Communist Party chief Jiang Zemin and other leaders to cut short trips to other parts of China and return to Beijing.
The mainland council's vice chairman, Shi Hwei-you, was cautious on the latest development in China.
"We are paying a close attention (to Deng's health), we also have countermeasures. But we don't want to speculate," Shi said on state television.
"We hope relations on the both sides of the Taiwan strait can develop steadily in any circumstances, and we also hope the mainland side can establish a democratic succession system."

Asked how Taiwan would react to Deng's death, Chang King-yuh told the United Daily News that the Mainland Affairs Council and other government agencies would be ready when it happened, but it was inappropriate to comment further before he actually dies.
Chang could not be reached for comment.
Analysts said rumours about Deng's death surface periodically and the fear of post-Deng uncertainty has eased on each occasion.
"I believe the impact (of Deng's death) will be much smaller than before," said Vincent Siew, a legislator from the ruling Nationalist party and former Mainland Affairs Council chairman.

Taiwan's usually hypersensitive stock market shrugged off reports on Deng's health. The stock index fell 2.11 percent at Tuesday's opening but rebounded to end only 45.15 points, or 0.59 percent, lower at 7,642.03.

Deng, 92, whose pragmatic policies transformed a backward Stalinist state into an economic powerhouse, lives in a tightly guarded compound behind the Forbidden City of China's emperors in central Beijing.

Diplomats have said one barometer of Deng's health in China's highly secretive system was the movements of top leaders and close family members, with few willing to be out of town or abroad if Deng were close to death.

Deng has not been seen in public since the 1994 Chinese Lunar New Year festival when he appeared frail and faltering on a visit to Shanghai. He is now believed to be in fragile health and with fading lucidity.
